title: In the Beginning
subtitle: Genesis in Poems & Pictures
beforeYouBegin:
Genesis runs from the first light to a coffin in Egypt: a garden, a flood, a family that God promises to bless, and the long, tangled story of how he keeps that promise through liars, wrestlers, and brothers who sold their brother.

This book walks through it in forty short poems, in four parts. Each poem sits beside a picture and under a single line of Scripture. It doesn't cover every chapter; it stops at the moments that carry the story.

The poems are not the Bible. They are one reader's response to it. Open Genesis alongside this book, and let the real words have the last word.

parts.title: Part One · In the Beginning
parts.epigraph: In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth.

parts.title: Part Two · The Friend of God
parts.epigraph: Go to the land that I will show you.

parts.title: Part Three · Wrestling
parts.epigraph: Your name will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel

parts.title: Part Four · God Meant It for Good
parts.epigraph: You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good

paintings.title: let there be
paintings.poem:
before anything,
a voice
over dark water.
no struggle.
no battle with the deep.
just a sentence—
and light
did what it was told,
and has been doing it
every morning since.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Before you rush into the tasks of the day, look at the morning light outside your window: what chaos in your life needs not a battle from you, but a single quiet word from the One who spoke over dark water?

paintings.title: very good
paintings.poem:
six times he stepped back
and said: good.
the light. the land.
the seas and the seeds.
the lights in the sky.
the swimmers and the fliers.
the cattle and the creeping things.
and at the end,
looking at all of it,
with us in it:
very good.
remember that
on the days
you forget it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Six times He said “good,” and with us in the picture He said “very good”—what part of your ordinary life or your own reflection have you been judging harshly that God still calls good?

paintings.title: the gallery
paintings.poem:
every face you pass today
was made to look like someone.
not like a king.
not like a statue in a temple.
like God.
the beggar and the boss,
the man and the woman,
the neighbor you avoid—
you are walking
through a gallery
of his image.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Think of the next difficult or overlooked person you will cross paths with today: how would your posture shift if you remembered you are walking past a living portrait in God’s own gallery?

paintings.title: the seventh day
paintings.poem:
he finished,
and then he stopped.
not because he was tired.
because rest
was part of the making.
the first thing God called holy
wasn't a place.
it was a day
with nothing to do.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The crown of creation was not another achievement, but a day with nothing to do—what one striving can you lay down on the stone bench today simply to delight in what is already finished?

paintings.title: dust and breath
paintings.poem:
his name is a play on words:
Adam,
from adamah,
the ground.
we are dirt
that God leaned close to
and breathed on.
so be humble—
you're dust.
and be amazed—
you're breathed.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause right now and take one slow, unhurried breath: what changes when you remember you are not a machine running down, but dust held together this very second by the breath of God?

paintings.title: not good
paintings.poem:
everything was good,
until God noticed
one thing that wasn't.
not sin. not yet.
just a man
with no one beside him.
the first "not good"
in the Bible
is loneliness.
God took it seriously.
so should we.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: When you feel the ache of doing something alone, who has God placed beside you as a companion—and how can you thank them today before the sun goes down?

paintings.title: where are you?
paintings.poem:
he knew where they were.
the question wasn't for him.
it was for them—
crouched among the trees,
sewing leaves,
ashamed of their own skin.
where are you?
not a hunter's shout.
a father's call
at evening,
walking the garden
the way he always did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: “Where are you?” was not the shout of a detective, but the heartbreak of a Father walking through the cool of the trees: what fig leaves of excuses or busyness are keeping you from stepping out into the open with Him today?

paintings.title: clothed
paintings.poem:
there were consequences—
thorns, sweat,
the long road out.
but before they left,
God knelt
and made them clothes.
theirfig leaves
weren't enough.
his mercy
was.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Even as they left the garden, God knelt to stitch garments for the ones who broke His heart—how have you felt His quiet covering over you even inside the consequences of a mistake?

paintings.title: keeper
paintings.poem:
the first question was:
where are you?
the second:
where is your brother?
Cain shrugged.
am I supposed to keep track of him?
yes.
that is exactly
what you were for.
and the ground itself
would not stay quiet.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: “Am I my brother’s keeper?” still echoes whenever we look away from another’s need: whose burden or loneliness near you today is God gently asking you to notice and share?

paintings.title: one green leaf
paintings.poem:
the first time, she came back
with nothing.
the second time, at evening,
a leaf.
fresh. green.
torn from a living tree.
that's all.
not the end of the flood—
proof that it was ending.
sometimes hope
is one small green thing
carried a long way.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: After forty days of rain and long waiting, hope arrived as one small olive leaf in a dove’s beak: what small green sign of renewal is God already sending into your waiting season?

paintings.title: the bow in the cloud
paintings.poem:
a warrior's bow,
hung up
in the clouds.
and God said:
when I see it,
I will remember.
not you—
I.
the promise doesn't depend
on your memory.
it hangs on his.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: God hung His warrior’s bow in the clouds pointed away from the earth: when the storm finally passes, what altar of gratitude can you stack on the wet ground?

paintings.title: a name for ourselves
paintings.poem:
come, let's build.
let's reach the sky.
let's make a name—
the oldest plan in the world.
they wanted height.
God wanted them spread across the earth.
a chapter later,
he calls one man
and says:
I will make your name great.
the name you build
falls.
the name you're given
stands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Tower-builders reach for a name so they won’t be scattered; pilgrims leave with only a promise—where are you trying to build a monument to your own security instead of listening for His call?

paintings.title: go
paintings.poem:
leave.
your country.
your family.
your father's house.
go.
where?
I'll show you.
no map,
only a voice—
and a seventy- five-year-old man
packs his tents.
faith often starts
with not knowing
where.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Abram walked out without a map, knowing only the Voice who said “Go”: what next step are you postponing until you can see mile ten, when God is only asking you to take step one?

paintings.title: count them
paintings.poem:
he was old,
and had no son,
and God took him outside
and said: look up.
count them.
he couldn't.
that was the point.
and he believed—
and God counted that
as righteousness.
the first thing faith does
is step outside
and look up.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Step outside tonight and look up at the sky if you can: what promise of God feels too vast for your small tent right now?

paintings.title: the God who sees
paintings.poem:
Hagar—
a slave, a foreigner,
pregnant, mistreated,
run away into the desert.
nobody's first choice.
and God found her by a spring
and called her by name.
and she gave God a name
no one had given him before:
the God who sees.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: By the desert spring, a runaway servant gave God a name—“You are the God who sees”: what unseen corner of your week does it comfort you to know He has never looked away from?

paintings.title: too hard
paintings.poem:
she laughed
inside the tent,
the way you laugh
at a promise that's come too late.
old.
worn out.
done hoping.
and a voice outside asked:
is anything too hard for the Lord?
that question is still standing
in the doorway
of every tent
where someone stopped hoping.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “too hard” (Genesis 18:10-14), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the still, unhurried voice after reading, “that question is still standing in the doorway of every tent where someone stopped hoping”?

paintings.title: laughter
paintings.poem:
she named him Laughter—
Isaac.
the same laugh
that once meant
I don't believe it
now means
I can't believe it.
God doesn't scold her.
he gives her a son
and a better reason
to laugh.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“she named him Laughter— Isaac”) and the closing thought (“he gives her a son and a better reason to laugh”), what is Genesis 21:1-7 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: the Lord will provide
paintings.poem:
where is the lamb, father?
God will provide, my son.
and they walked on,
the two of them together,
up the mountain.
this is the hardest chapter
in the book,
and the story tells it
in a hush.
but it ends
with a ram in the thicket
and a new name for the mountain:
the Lord will provide.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of In the Beginning, “the Lord will provide” (Genesis 22:7-14) slows us down at the long climb up the hill to remind us: “but it ends with a ram in the thicket and a new name for the mountain: the Lord will provide.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: the camels too
paintings.poem:
a stranger asked for a drink.
she gave it.
then she said:
I'll water your camels too—
ten thirsty camels,
jar after jar
from the well.
the servant had prayed for a sign.
he got a young woman
who did more
than she was asked.
that is often
how God answers:
through someone's
generous hands.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “the camels too” (Genesis 24:15-20), what would you talk about after reading, “that is often how God answers: through someone's generous hands”?

paintings.title: full of years
paintings.poem:
he left home at seventy- five
on a promise.
he did not see
the nation,
the land,
the stars made good.
he saw one son,
a burial cave,
and a lifetime of God
keeping his word
a little at a time.
and he died
full of years.
not empty.
full.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet stars overhead: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “full of years”—“and he died full of years. not empty. full”?

paintings.title: red stew
paintings.poem:
he came in starving
and traded his future
for a bowl of red stew.
it tasted good.
it was gone in minutes.
don't laugh at Esau too quickly.
we all have a bowl
we'd sell tomorrow
for tonight.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the steaming bowl traded for a birthright in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “we all have a bowl we'd sell tomorrow for tonight” (Genesis 25:29-34)?

paintings.title: the stairway
paintings.poem:
he was running
from a brother he had cheated,
sleeping on the ground
with a stone for a pillow.
and heaven
came down a stairway
to meet him there.
not because he had earned it.
because God had promised,
and does not wait
for us to deserve it.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Genesis 28:10-15, the story turns on the stone pillow at the foot of the stairway—and ends with, “because God had promised, and does not wait for us to deserve it.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: I didn't know it
paintings.poem:
God was here,
and I didn't know it.
maybe the most honest sentence
anyone ever said
waking up.
so he set up the stone
and poured oil on it
to remember:
the lonely place,
the hard ground,
the night I ran—
God was here.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Genesis 28:16-18 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “I didn't know it” and whispers, “so he set up the stone and poured oil on it to remember: the lonely place, the hard ground, the night I ran— God was here.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: a few days
paintings.poem:
seven years of work
for Rachel.
and the book says
they went by
like a few days.
love does strange things
to the clock.
the story after this
is not simple.
the book won't pretend it is.
but this line
is true.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “the story after this is not simple. but this line is true.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: until the day breaks
paintings.poem:
alone at the river,
at night,
someone takes hold of him,
and he fights back
till dawn.
he's wrestled all his life—
his brother, his father,
his uncle, his fear.
now he wrestles God
and won't let go:
not until you bless me.
it is the most Jacob thing
he ever said,
and the most faithful.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “it is the most Jacob thing he ever said, and the most faithful” (Genesis 32:24-26) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: the limp
paintings.poem:
he walked away
blessed
and limping.
a new name.
a new way of walking.
some blessings
come with a limp,
so you never forget
who you met
by the river.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “the limp” (Genesis 32:30-31): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “some blessings come with a limp, so you never forget who you met by the river”?

paintings.title: Esau ran
paintings.poem:
twenty years of dread.
four hundred men coming.
gifts sent ahead in waves.
and then—
Esau ran.
not to fight.
to hold him.
the thing you feared most
may be running toward you
with open arms.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Genesis 33:1-4 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “the thing you feared most may be running toward you with open arms” in your own story?

paintings.title: the coat
paintings.poem:
a father's favorite,
and everyone knew it.
the coat said so
every time he wore it.
love is good.
favoritism
tears a family
like cloth.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “the coat” (Genesis 37:3-4), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the torn and mended coat after reading, “favoritism tears a family like cloth”?

paintings.title: the empty pit
paintings.poem:
no water in it.
no way out.
seventeen,
and his brothers sit down to eat
on the rim.
this is where
the dream seems to die.
it doesn't.
it is going down
the way seeds go down.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Between the opening line (“no water in it. no way out”) and the closing thought (“it is going down the way seeds go down”), what is Genesis 37:23-25 gently reframing in your own day?

paintings.title: the refrain
paintings.poem:
sold as a slave:
the Lord was with Joseph.
falsely accused:
the Lord was with Joseph.
thrown in prison:
the Lord was with Joseph.
the chapter keeps saying it,
like a drumbeat
under the worst years of his life.
the circumstances change.
the refrain
doesn't.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Along the road of In the Beginning, “the refrain” (Genesis 39:2-23) slows us down at the quiet centerpiece of “the refrain” to remind us: “the circumstances change. the refrain doesn't.” Where are you being invited to trade control for trust today?

paintings.title: forgotten
paintings.poem:
remember me, Joseph said,
when it goes well for you.
and it went well for him.
and he forgot.
two more years
in the dark.
if you've been forgotten
by someone who promised,
you are not forgotten
by the One who did.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: If you were walking this road with a close friend and stopped at “forgotten” (Genesis 40:14-23), what would you talk about after reading, “if you've been forgotten by someone who promised, you are not forgotten by the One who did”?

paintings.title: not in me
paintings.poem:
shaved, dressed,
pulled from the prison,
he stands before the king of Egypt,
who says:
I hear you can interpret dreams.
it's his big chance.
and his first words are:
it isn't in me.
the most useful people God has
are the ones
who know
where the gift came from.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Pause before the quiet centerpiece of “not in me”: what changes in your posture today when you sit with the closing words of “not in me”—“the most useful people God has are the ones who know where the gift came from”?

paintings.title: faces to the earth
paintings.poem:
they came for grain
and bowed to the governor
with their faces in the dust.
they didn't know him.
he knew them.
the dream from the field,
the sheaves bowing down—
come true
in a way
nobody wanted anymore.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Look at the stillness of the dust of the road in Timothy’s painting: what striving can you lay down as you ponder, “the dream from the field, the sheaves bowing down— come true in a way nobody wanted anymore” (Genesis 42:6-8)?

paintings.title: instead of the boy
paintings.poem:
Judah—
the brother who once said
let's sell him—
now says:
take me instead.
let the boy go home.
it would kill our father.
that's how Joseph knew
they had changed.
a man who once sold a brother
now offers himself
for one.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: In Genesis 44:30-34, the story turns on the quiet centerpiece of “instead of the boy”—and ends with, “a man who once sold a brother now offers himself for one.” What small, unhurried faithfulness is God inviting you into today?

paintings.title: come near
paintings.poem:
he sent everyone out
and wept so loud
the Egyptians heard it.
I am Joseph.
and they couldn't speak.
then the gentlest words
in the whole long story:
come near to me.
please.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The world measures life by speed and noise, yet Genesis 45:1-4 points us to the quiet centerpiece of “come near” and whispers, “then the gentlest words in the whole long story: come near to me. please.” How can you practice that unhurried wisdom today?

paintings.title: sent
paintings.poem:
don't be angry with yourselves,
he said.
you sold me.
God sent me.
both are true.
he doesn't pretend
the first one didn't happen.
he just refuses
to let it be
the whole story.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: The poem closes with a quiet turn: “he just refuses to let it be the whole story.” Where in your life right now does that line hit closest to home?

paintings.title: the wagons
paintings.poem:
Joseph is alive, they said,
and the old man
didn't believe them.
then he saw the wagons.
sometimes it isn't the words
that raise a heart.
it's the wagons—
proof you can touch
that someone
is coming to carry you.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Sometimes a single sentence opens a window in a closed room: how does “it's the wagons— proof you can touch that someone is coming to carry you” (Genesis 45:25-28) speak to a question you have been carrying lately?

paintings.title: a good while
paintings.poem:
twenty-two years.
a chariot racing up from Egypt,
an old man leaning on his staff,
and the book, usually so brisk,
slows down:
he wept on his neck
a good while.
some reunions
you don't hurry.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Hold your hands open for a moment before “a good while” (Genesis 46:28-30): what are you gripping tightly that loosens when you hear, “some reunions you don't hurry”?

paintings.title: underneath
paintings.poem:
you meant it for evil.
God meant it for good.
not: it wasn't evil.
not: it didn't hurt.
but underneath the worst thing
anyone ever did to him,
another hand
was working
the whole time.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: Scripture remembers this moment in Genesis 50:15-21 not to impress us, but to steady us: when have you seen the truth that “but underneath the worst thing anyone ever did to him, another hand was working the whole time” in your own story?

paintings.title: the road home
paintings.poem:
the book that began
with light and a garden
ends
with a coffin in Egypt.
but not with despair.
Joseph's last words:
God will surely come for you.
take my bones with you
when you go.
Genesis ends
with a promise,
and bones ready
for the road home.
paintings.reflectionPrompt: As your pilgrim lantern pauses at “the road home” (Genesis 50:24-26), what one honest sentence would you pray beside the quiet centerpiece of “the road home” after reading, “Genesis ends with a promise, and bones ready for the road home”?
